prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The presence of dust at high redshift requires efficient condensation of grains in SN ejecta, in accordance with current theoretical models. Yet, observations of the few well studied SNe and SN remnants imply condensation efficiencies which are about two orders of magnitude smaller. Motivated by this tension, we have (i) revisited the model of Todini & Ferrara (2001) for dust formation in the ejecta of core collapse SNe and (ii) followed, for the first time, the evolution of newly condensed grains from the time of formation to their survival - through the passage of the reverse shock - in the SN remnant. We find that 0.1 - 0.6 M_sun of dust form in the ejecta of 12 - 40 M_sun stellar progenitors. Depending on the density of the surrounding ISM, between 2-20% of the initial dust mass survives the passage of the reverse shock, on time-scales of about 4-8 x 10^4 yr from the stellar explosion. Sputtering by the hot gas induces a shift of the dust size distribution towards smaller grains. The resulting dust extinction curve shows a good agreement with that derived by observations of a reddened QSO at z =6.2. Stochastic heating of small grains leads to a wide distribution of dust temperatures. This supports the idea that large amounts (~ 0.1 M_sun) of cold dust (T ~ 40K) can be present in SN remnants, without being in conflict with the observed IR emission.

outputs.L1:
The presence of dust at high redshift requires efficient grain condensation in supernova ejecta, consistent with current theoretical models. However, observations of the few well-studied supernovae and supernova remnants suggest condensation efficiencies approximately two orders of magnitude lower. Motivated by this tension, we have (i) revisited the dust-formation model of Todini & Ferrara (2001) for the ejecta of core-collapse supernovae and (ii) followed, for the first time, the evolution of newly condensed grains from their formation to their survival—through the passage of the reverse shock—in the supernova remnant.

We find that 0.1–0.6 M_sun of dust forms in the ejecta of 12–40 M_sun stellar progenitors. Depending on the density of the surrounding interstellar medium, 2–20% of the initial dust mass survives the passage of the reverse shock, on timescales of about 4–8 x 10^4 yr after the stellar explosion. Sputtering by the hot gas shifts the dust-size distribution toward smaller grains. The resulting dust-extinction curve agrees well with that derived from observations of a reddened QSO at z = 6.2. Stochastic heating of small grains leads to a broad distribution of dust temperatures, supporting the idea that large amounts (~0.1 M_sun) of cold dust (T ~ 40 K) can be present in supernova remnants without conflicting with the observed IR emission.
outputs.L2:
Dust observed at very large redshifts implies that grains must condense efficiently within supernova ejecta, as predicted by present theoretical models. However, measurements from the small number of well-studied supernovae and supernova remnants suggest condensation efficiencies roughly one hundred times lower. To address this discrepancy, we have (i) re-examined the dust-formation model of Todini & Ferrara (2001) for ejecta from core-collapse supernovae and (ii) traced, for the first time, the development of newly formed grains from their initial condensation through their survival after the reverse shock passes through the supernova remnant.

Our results indicate that ejecta from stellar progenitors of 12–40 M_sun produce about 0.1–0.6 M_sun of dust. The fraction of this original dust mass that remains after the reverse shock depends on the density of the surrounding interstellar medium, with approximately 2–20% surviving over timescales of about 4–8 × 10^4 years after the explosion. Sputtering caused by hot gas shifts the grain-size distribution toward smaller particles. The extinction curve produced by the surviving dust is in strong agreement with that inferred from observations of a reddened quasar at z = 6.2. In addition, stochastic heating of small grains generates a broad range of dust temperatures. This finding supports the possibility that supernova remnants may contain substantial quantities, around 0.1 M_sun, of cold dust at T ~ 40 K without contradicting the infrared emission that has been observed.
outputs.L3:
The presence of significant amounts of dust at high redshift implies that dust must have formed rapidly in the early Universe. Since low- and intermediate-mass stars require relatively long evolutionary timescales before they can contribute dust through stellar winds, core-collapse supernovae are often considered a major early source of dust. To explain the observed dust masses in distant galaxies and quasars, supernova ejecta would need to condense grains with high efficiency. However, direct observations of nearby supernovae and young supernova remnants have often indicated much lower dust condensation efficiencies, creating an apparent tension between theoretical requirements and observational evidence.

This study revisits a model of dust formation in the ejecta of core-collapse supernovae and follows the subsequent evolution of the newly formed grains as they encounter the reverse shock in supernova remnants. After a supernova explosion, the expanding ejecta eventually interacts with the surrounding interstellar medium. This interaction drives a forward shock into the ambient gas and a reverse shock back into the ejecta. The reverse shock heats and processes the ejecta, subjecting newly formed dust grains to sputtering, erosion, and possible destruction. Therefore, the amount of dust initially produced in the ejecta is not necessarily the same as the amount that ultimately survives and is injected into the interstellar medium.

The models considered in the study predict that substantial quantities of dust can form in the ejecta of massive stellar progenitors. For core-collapse supernovae arising from stars with initial masses of approximately 12–40 solar masses, the initial dust mass is estimated to be about 0.1–0.6 solar masses. This suggests that, at least in principle, supernovae are capable of producing enough dust to contribute significantly to the dust budget of young galaxies, provided that a sufficient fraction of this material can survive later processing.

However, the survival of dust grains depends strongly on the density of the surrounding interstellar medium. In denser environments, the reverse shock is stronger and more destructive, leading to more efficient sputtering and grain destruction. In lower-density environments, grains are processed less severely and a larger fraction can survive. According to the models, only about 2–20% of the initial dust mass remains after the reverse shock has passed through the ejecta, over timescales of roughly 40,000–80,000 years. This means that while supernovae may form large amounts of dust initially, most of that dust can be destroyed before it is delivered to the wider interstellar medium.

The study also examines how the reverse shock alters the grain size distribution, extinction properties, and thermal emission of the surviving dust. Smaller grains are preferentially destroyed, leaving behind a population biased toward larger grains. This evolution changes the expected extinction curves and affects the equilibrium temperatures of the dust grains. Importantly, the predicted temperatures and infrared emission properties are consistent with the idea that supernova remnants may contain substantial masses of cold dust. Such cold dust could remain difficult to detect at shorter infrared wavelengths, meaning that large dust masses in remnants would not necessarily conflict with existing infrared observations.

Overall, the results support a picture in which core-collapse supernovae can form significant amounts of dust, but only a modest fraction survives the destructive effects of the reverse shock. Even so, the surviving dust may still represent an important contribution to the interstellar dust reservoir, especially in the early Universe.
outputs.L4:
The study investigates how core-collapse supernovae could have contributed to the large amounts of dust observed in galaxies at high redshift. Observations of the early Universe imply that substantial dust masses were already present within a relatively short time after the first generations of stars formed. However, this requirement appears to be in tension with the comparatively low dust condensation efficiencies inferred from some nearby supernova observations. To address this problem, the study revisits theoretical models of dust formation in the ejecta of core-collapse supernovae and follows the subsequent evolution of the newly formed dust as it passes through the hostile environment of a supernova remnant.

In the models considered, dust grains condense in the metal-rich ejecta after the explosion. The amount and composition of the dust depend on the properties of the progenitor star, the structure of the ejecta, and the physical conditions during cooling. The calculations show that core-collapse supernovae can initially form substantial quantities of dust, typically in the range of about 0.1 to 0.6 solar masses. This suggests that the dust production phase itself can be efficient enough to account for the large dust reservoirs inferred in young galaxies.

The study then examines what happens to this dust when the reverse shock propagates back into the expanding ejecta. The reverse shock heats and compresses the gas and can destroy grains through sputtering and grain–gas collisions. The survival rate of dust is therefore not determined solely by how much dust forms, but also by the density of the surrounding interstellar medium and the resulting strength of shock processing. In denser environments, the reverse shock is more destructive, while in lower-density environments a larger fraction of the grains can survive.

The results indicate that roughly 2–20% of the initially formed dust survives the reverse-shock phase, depending mainly on the ambient interstellar density. Although this survival fraction is modest, the initial dust masses are large enough that core-collapse supernovae can still inject significant quantities of dust into the interstellar medium. This supports the idea that supernovae were important dust sources in the early Universe, especially before lower-mass stars had time to evolve and contribute dust through asymptotic giant branch winds.

The study also helps explain several observational features of supernova remnants. The formation of relatively large amounts of cold dust in the ejecta is consistent with far-infrared and submillimetre detections of dust in young remnants. At the same time, the processing and partial destruction of grains by the reverse shock can account for the lower dust masses inferred in some older remnants. The models also provide a framework for interpreting observed extinction properties, since the size distribution and composition of surviving grains influence how they absorb and scatter light.

Overall, the study concludes that core-collapse supernovae can reconcile the high dust masses observed in the early Universe with the lower apparent dust yields measured in some local remnants. Even after significant destruction by reverse shocks, enough dust can survive to make supernovae major contributors to cosmic dust enrichment, particularly during the first billion years of galaxy evolution.
outputs.L5:
**The Mystery of SNe**

The universe is full of powerful events, yet few are as dramatic as SNe, or supernovae. These stellar explosions occur when certain stars reach the end of their lives, releasing enormous amounts of energy and light. For a short time, a single supernova can shine brighter than an entire galaxy.

Yet SNe are not only destructive. They also help create and spread heavy elements such as iron, calcium, and gold across space. These elements later become part of new stars, planets, and even living organisms. In this way, supernovae play an important role in the cycle of cosmic creation.

The study of SNe helps scientists understand how stars evolve, how galaxies change, and how the universe expands. Although these explosions happen far away, their influence reaches across time and space, reminding us that even endings can lead to new beginnings.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astrophysics paper about dust formation in core-collapse supernova ejecta, survival through reverse shocks, and implications for high-redshift quasars.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are leading candidates for the rapid production of dust in the early Universe, where large dust masses are inferred in galaxies and quasars at redshifts \(z \gtrsim 6\), before low-mass asymptotic giant branch stars can contribute substantially. We investigate dust formation in metal-rich CCSN ejecta and its subsequent processing by the reverse shock as the remnant expands into the surrounding medium. Using ejecta models spanning a range of progenitor masses, explosion energies, and ambient densities, we follow the condensation of refractory species, the evolution of grain-size distributions, and the destruction of grains by thermal sputtering and grain-grain processing in shocked gas. We find that CCSNe can form substantial dust masses in the freely expanding ejecta, but the surviving fraction is highly sensitive to the initial grain-size distribution, ejecta mixing, explosion structure, and circumstellar environment. Small grains are efficiently destroyed, while larger grains and grains formed in dense clumps can survive reverse-shock processing and be injected into the interstellar medium. For plausible early-galaxy conditions, the net dust yield per CCSN can remain significant, though typically lower than the freshly condensed dust mass by factors of several to orders of magnitude. These results imply that CCSNe can contribute meaningfully to the dust budgets of high-redshift quasars, but may require efficient grain growth in the interstellar medium or favorable supernova environments to explain the largest observed dust masses. Our study highlights the importance of coupling dust formation models to remnant-scale shock evolution and provides constraints on the role of massive stars in enriching the earliest galaxies with dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that revisits the Todini & Ferrara (2001) model of supernova dust formation and tracks grain survival in supernova remnants, including key quantitative results.
counterfactuals.output:
The study is most likely **Bianchi & Schneider (2007), “Dust formation and survival in supernova ejecta”**, which explicitly revisits the **Todini & Ferrara (2001; TF01)** core-collapse supernova dust-formation model and then follows how much of the newly formed dust survives processing by the reverse shock in the supernova remnant.

### Aim

The paper reassesses whether core-collapse supernovae can be major dust producers, especially at high redshift, by asking two linked questions:

1. **How much dust forms in the SN ejecta?**  
   This updates/revisits the TF01 classical nucleation and grain-growth calculation.

2. **How much of that dust survives the reverse shock?**  
   Newly formed grains are exposed to thermal and non-thermal sputtering in the shocked ejecta, which can destroy a large fraction of the initial dust yield.

---

## Model setup

### Dust formation

The authors use a TF01-style model for dust condensation in expanding SN ejecta. They consider core-collapse progenitors with masses of roughly

\[
12-40 \, M_\odot
\]

and different initial metallicities, including solar and low-metallicity cases.

The main dust species formed include:

- amorphous carbon,
- silicates such as forsterite/enstatite-like grains,
- magnetite,
- corundum/alumina,
- silica and other oxide grains depending on ejecta composition.

The model assumes onion-shell ejecta structure rather than complete microscopic mixing, so different grain species condense in chemically distinct zones.

---

## Initial dust yields before remnant processing

A key result is that core-collapse SNe can form large dust masses initially. The typical freshly condensed dust mass is of order

\[
M_{\rm dust,0} \sim 0.1-0.6 \, M_\odot
\]

depending on progenitor mass, explosion properties, and metallicity.

The condensation efficiency can be high, with a substantial fraction of refractory elements locked into dust soon after the explosion.

However, the predicted grain-size distribution is heavily weighted toward small grains. Many grains have radii

\[
a \lesssim 0.01 \, \mu{\rm m},
\]

which is important because small grains are especially vulnerable to sputtering in the supernova remnant.

---

## Reverse-shock processing

The authors then follow the passage of the reverse shock through the ejecta and calculate dust destruction by sputtering. The survival fraction depends strongly on the density of the surrounding interstellar medium.

They examine ambient hydrogen densities such as

\[
n_{\rm H} = 0.1,\; 1,\; 10 \, {\rm cm^{-3}}.
\]

The main finding is that the reverse shock can destroy most of the initially formed dust, especially the smallest grains.

Approximate survival fractions are:

- For a low-density medium,  
  \[
  n_{\rm H} \sim 0.1 \, {\rm cm^{-3}},
  \]
  a significant fraction can survive, roughly tens of percent and in favorable cases up to nearly the original dust mass.

- For a typical diffuse ISM density,  
  \[
  n_{\rm H} \sim 1 \, {\rm cm^{-3}},
  \]
  only about
  \[
  \sim 2\%-20\%
  \]
  of the original dust mass survives.

- For a dense medium,  
  \[
  n_{\rm H} \sim 10 \, {\rm cm^{-3}},
  \]
  destruction is severe and almost all newly formed dust can be sputtered away.

In mass terms, after reverse-shock processing the surviving dust mass is typically reduced to roughly

\[
M_{\rm dust,surv} \sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1} \, M_\odot
\]

per supernova, depending on ambient density and progenitor model.

---

## Grain-size effects

The reverse shock strongly modifies the size distribution.

- Small grains are preferentially destroyed.
- Larger grains survive more efficiently because their sputtering lifetimes scale roughly with grain radius.
- The post-shock dust population is therefore biased toward larger grains compared with the initial ejecta distribution.

This means that the dust mass survival fraction is not simply a fixed number; it depends sensitively on the initial grain-size distribution predicted by the formation model.

---

## Implications

The study concludes that while supernovae may form large amounts of dust initially, the **effective dust yield injected into the ISM is much smaller** once reverse-shock destruction is included.

A representative conclusion is:

\[
M_{\rm dust,formed} \sim 0.1-0.6 \, M_\odot
\]

but

\[
M_{\rm dust,surviving} \sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1} \, M_\odot.
\]

Thus, core-collapse SNe can contribute to dust enrichment, especially in the early Universe, but they are less efficient net dust producers than implied by formation calculations alone. The paper emphasizes that reverse-shock destruction must be included when using SNe to explain the large dust masses observed in young galaxies and high-redshift quasars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise scientific abstract explaining how supernovae can produce and preserve enough dust to account for observations of dust at high redshift.
counterfactuals.output: Supernovae are potentially major dust factories in the early universe, where evolved low-mass stars have not yet had time to contribute substantially. In the rapidly cooling ejecta of core-collapse supernovae, refractory elements synthesized in the explosion can condense into dust grains on timescales of months to years. Infrared and submillimeter observations of nearby remnants indicate that some supernovae can form large dust masses, up to ~0.1–1 solar masses, sufficient in principle to explain the abundant dust observed in galaxies at high redshift. A key uncertainty is survival: the reverse shock driven back into the ejecta can sputter and shatter newly formed grains. However, survival is enhanced if grains grow to relatively large sizes, are concentrated in dense clumps, or form in regions shielded from the hottest shocked gas. Models including clumpy ejecta, rapid grain growth, and partial reverse-shock destruction find that a significant fraction of the initial dust mass can remain and later be injected into the interstellar medium. Combined with subsequent grain growth in dense interstellar clouds, supernova dust production can plausibly account for the large dust reservoirs detected within the first billion years after the Big Bang.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract with numerical findings on dust masses formed in 12–40 solar-mass SN progenitors, reverse shock destruction in different ISM densities, and resulting extinction curves.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract** — We investigate dust formation, reverse-shock processing, and the resulting extinction properties of core-collapse supernovae arising from 12–40 \(M_\odot\) progenitors. Using ejecta models spanning 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 40 \(M_\odot\), we find that freshly condensed dust masses increase with progenitor mass from \(\sim 0.08\,M_\odot\) for a 12 \(M_\odot\) progenitor to \(\sim 0.7\,M_\odot\) for a 40 \(M_\odot\) progenitor, with typical grain radii of \(10^{-3}\)–\(10^{-1}\,\mu{\rm m}\). The dominant condensates are silicates, amorphous carbon, magnetite, alumina, and Si-bearing grains, with the relative composition set by the ejecta stratification and degree of microscopic mixing. Subsequent interaction with the reverse shock substantially reduces the surviving dust mass. For a diffuse ambient medium with \(n_{\rm H}=0.1\,{\rm cm^{-3}}\), \(35\)–\(80\%\) of the initial dust survives, leaving \(\sim 0.03\)–\(0.45\,M_\odot\). At \(n_{\rm H}=1\,{\rm cm^{-3}}\), survival fractions fall to \(10\)–\(40\%\), while dense environments with \(n_{\rm H}=10\,{\rm cm^{-3}}\) destroy nearly all small grains and leave only \(\lesssim 1\)–\(10\%\) of the initial dust, corresponding to surviving masses of \(\sim 10^{-3}\)–\(5\times10^{-2}\,M_\odot\). Grain sputtering preferentially removes particles smaller than \(\sim 0.03\,\mu{\rm m}\), producing a flatter post-shock size distribution and shifting the opacity toward larger grains. The predicted extinction curves before shock processing are steep in the ultraviolet, with \(A_\lambda/A_V\) at \(0.15\,\mu{\rm m}\) reaching \(\sim 4\)–8 depending on progenitor mass and composition. After reverse-shock destruction, the extinction curves become progressively greyer, especially for \(n_{\rm H}\geq1\,{\rm cm^{-3}}\), where the UV-to-optical contrast is reduced by factors of \(\sim 2\)–4 and the 2175 Å feature remains weak or absent unless carbonaceous grains dominate. These results indicate that supernovae can form large dust masses initially, but their net contribution to interstellar dust budgets and high-redshift extinction depends sensitively on the circumstellar and interstellar gas density into which the remnant expands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal astrophysics language, describe the tension between theoretical supernova dust condensation efficiencies and observations, and present model results for dust formation, sputtering, survival fractions, and infrared emission in SN remnants.
counterfactuals.output:
Theoretical models of dust nucleation in core-collapse supernovae often predict very efficient condensation of refractory material in the freely expanding metal-rich ejecta, whereas direct observational constraints have historically implied substantially smaller warm-dust masses. This discrepancy constitutes a major tension in supernova dust studies: supernovae are theoretically capable of being important dust factories, particularly at high redshift, but the amount of dust that forms, survives the reverse shock, and is ultimately injected into the interstellar medium remains uncertain.

In classical chemical-kinetic and equilibrium condensation calculations, a large fraction of the available refractory elements in the ejecta can condense into solid grains. For typical Type II-P or stripped-envelope core-collapse supernova progenitors, predicted newly formed dust masses are often of order

\[
M_{\rm d,0} \sim 10^{-2} - 1\,M_\odot ,
\]

depending on progenitor mass, explosion energy, ejecta mixing, molecule formation, grain composition, and the degree of clumping. In contrast, early mid-infrared observations of young supernovae frequently inferred only

\[
M_{\rm d,obs} \sim 10^{-5} - 10^{-3}\,M_\odot
\]

of warm dust at temperatures of several hundred kelvin. Such estimates are sensitive mainly to optically thin warm dust and can miss a much larger reservoir of cold dust radiating at far-infrared and submillimetre wavelengths. Later observations of remnants such as SN 1987A, Cassiopeia A, and the Crab Nebula have indeed revealed larger cold-dust masses, typically

\[
M_{\rm d,cold} \sim 10^{-2} - 10^{-1}\,M_\odot ,
\]

and in some interpretations approaching several tenths of a solar mass. Nevertheless, these inferred masses remain model-dependent because of uncertainties in dust opacity, temperature distributions, synchrotron subtraction, foreground contamination, and grain composition.

A further complication is that the initial condensation efficiency is not equivalent to the dust yield injected into the ambient interstellar medium. After formation in the expanding ejecta, grains are processed by the reverse shock driven into the ejecta as the forward shock sweeps up circumstellar and interstellar gas. Thermal and non-thermal sputtering, grain-grain collisions, shattering, and vaporisation can destroy a substantial fraction of the newly condensed dust. The surviving mass depends strongly on the ambient gas density, explosion energy, ejecta structure, grain-size distribution, and the degree of clumping.

In a typical supernova-remnant dust-processing calculation, the evolution may be summarised schematically as follows. Dust forms in the cool dense ejecta after a few hundred to several thousand days, with silicates, amorphous carbon, alumina, metallic iron, iron sulphides, and oxides condensing in chemically distinct zones. For an initial dust mass

\[
M_{\rm d,0} \sim 0.1 - 0.5\,M_\odot ,
\]

reverse-shock processing may reduce the surviving dust mass to

\[
M_{\rm d,surv} \sim 10^{-3} - 10^{-1}\,M_\odot .
\]

The corresponding survival fraction is therefore

\[
f_{\rm surv} =
\frac{M_{\rm d,surv}}{M_{\rm d,0}}
\sim 0.01 - 0.5 ,
\]

with low values occurring for small grains in dense ambient media and high values occurring for large grains embedded in dense ejecta clumps or expanding into low-density surroundings.

Small grains are particularly vulnerable because their sputtering lifetimes scale approximately with grain radius,

\[
\tau_{\rm sput} \propto \frac{a}{n_{\rm gas}},
\]

where \(a\) is the grain radius and \(n_{\rm gas}\) is the post-shock gas density. Grains with radii

\[
a \lesssim 0.01\,\mu{\rm m}
\]

are often almost completely destroyed, whereas grains with

\[
a \gtrsim 0.05 - 0.1\,\mu{\rm m}
\]

can survive more efficiently, particularly if they are initially located in dense, radiatively cooling ejecta clumps. Thus, the final dust yield is controlled not only by the total condensed mass but also by the initial grain-size distribution.

Representative model results for a core-collapse supernova remnant may be expressed as follows:

| Quantity | Typical model value |
|---|---:|
| Initial condensed dust mass | \(10^{-2} - 1\,M_\odot\) |
| Warm dust inferred at early epochs | \(10^{-5} - 10^{-3}\,M_\odot\) |
| Cold dust in evolved remnants | \(10^{-2} - 10^{-1}\,M_\odot\) |
| Reverse-shock sputtered mass fraction | \(50 - 99\%\), depending on environment |
| Surviving dust fraction | \(1 - 50\%\) |
| Surviving dust mass | \(10^{-3} - 10^{-1}\,M_\odot\) |
| Dominant destruction mechanism | Thermal/non-thermal sputtering in shocked gas |
| Most robust grains | Large carbonaceous or silicate grains |
| Most vulnerable grains | Small grains, \(a \lesssim 0.01\,\mu{\rm m}\) |

The infrared emission from supernova dust is likewise strongly phase-dependent. In very young supernovae, the emission is dominated by newly condensed warm dust and by pre-existing circumstellar dust heated either radiatively by the supernova flash or collisionally by shocked gas. The spectral energy distribution typically peaks in the mid-infrared, with characteristic dust temperatures

\[
T_{\rm d} \sim 300 - 1000\,{\rm K}.
\]

At later remnant stages, the bulk of the dust may be colder, with

\[
T_{\rm d} \sim 20 - 100\,{\rm K},
\]

and the emission shifts to far-infrared and submillimetre wavelengths. Collisionally heated grains behind the forward and reverse shocks can produce strong mid- and far-infrared continuum emission. The modelled luminosity depends on the local electron density and temperature, grain composition, and grain-size distribution. The dust luminosity may be written schematically as

\[
L_\nu =
\int 4\pi\,\kappa_\nu(a, i)\,B_\nu[T_{\rm d}(a,i)]\,
\rho_{\rm d}(a,i)\,dV\,da\,di ,
\]

where \(\kappa_\nu\) is the mass absorption coefficient, \(B_\nu\) is the Planck function, \(T_{\rm d}\) is the grain temperature, and the integral is taken over grain size, composition, and emitting volume.

The central astrophysical issue is therefore not whether dust can condense in supernova ejecta, but whether enough of it survives subsequent remnant processing to make supernovae significant net contributors to the cosmic dust budget. High condensation efficiencies alone would allow core-collapse supernovae to explain the large dust masses observed in young galaxies and high-redshift quasars. However, if reverse-shock sputtering destroys most of the grains, the effective supernova dust yield may fall to

\[
M_{\rm d,ISM} \lesssim 10^{-3} - 10^{-2}\,M_\odot
\]

per event, in which case interstellar grain growth in dense molecular gas becomes necessary to account for galactic dust masses. If, conversely, clumping and large-grain formation permit survival fractions of tens of percent, then supernovae can remain important primary dust sources, particularly in early galaxies where asymptotic-giant-branch stars have not yet had time to dominate dust production.

Thus, the tension between theory and observation arises from three linked uncertainties: the true initial condensation efficiency in chemically and dynamically complex ejecta, the amount of cold dust hidden from early mid-infrared observations, and the efficiency of reverse-shock destruction before the grains are released into the interstellar medium. Current supernova-remnant models favour substantial dust formation in the ejecta, severe but incomplete sputtering by the reverse shock, survival fractions ranging from a few percent to several tens of percent, and infrared emission that evolves from warm mid-infrared ejecta emission to colder far-infrared and submillimetre radiation in mature remnants.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
